initial_objective:
Goal: analyze a public bike-share dataset to find clear, well-supported patterns in how people use the system over time, and write a short report.

Data: NYC Citi Bike monthly trip-history files, publicly available from the Citi Bike system data page (s3.amazonaws.com/tripdata). Use one or two recent full years (for example 2023 and 2024). Each row is one trip with start and stop timestamps, station IDs, and rider type. If the data is not available in the container, say so and stop rather than inventing data.

Questions to answer:
1. How does monthly trip volume vary across the year? Is there a clear seasonal peak and trough?
2. How does usage vary by day of week and hour of day? Compare weekdays and weekends, and identify commute peaks if present.
3. How do member and casual riders differ in these patterns?
4. Optional, if time allows: is daily trip count associated with temperature or precipitation? Use a public weather source for the same dates only if it is easy to get; otherwise skip this.

Method: clean obviously bad records (negative or extreme durations, missing timestamps) and report how many were removed. Use plots and simple summary statistics. Report uncertainty where it matters, and do not claim causation.

Good result: a short report with 3 to 5 findings, each backed by a figure or table, the data source and cleaning steps stated, and limitations noted (for example, the dataset covers only one city and the rider-type field changed definition over time).

Constraints: work only in the campaign container. Save code, figures and the final report to the output directory.

experiments.skill_used: Set up Python environment and download/convert Citi Bike 2023-2024 trip data

parameters.description: Environment facts found while planning (container 16c10c580dbd, workdir /app): /app is empty; Python 3.11 with pip but NO pandas/numpy/matplotlib/scipy/curl/unzip installed; 128 CPUs; ~112 GB free disk; outbound internet works from Python (urllib) to s3.amazonaws.com, pypi.org and archive-api.open-meteo.com. Steps: (1) mkdir /app/code /app/raw_2023 /app/raw_2024 /app/parquet /app/output/{figures,tables} (each raw download dir must start empty; keep scripts in /app/code, not in the raw dirs). pip install duckdb pandas numpy matplotlib scipy statsmodels pyarrow (duckdb is preferred for the ~35-45M-row-per-year data so memory is never a problem). (2) Download with Python urllib/requests (stream to disk, retry) the 12 monthly files https://s3.amazonaws.com/tripdata/2024MM-citibike-tripdata.zip (MM=01..12; 0.4-1.0 GB each) into /app/raw_2024, and the single yearly archive https://s3.amazonaws.com/tripdata/2023-citibike-tripdata.zip (1.6 GB; 2023 monthly URLs return 404) into /app/raw_2023. Verified via HEAD requests that all of these exist. The 2023 yearly zip likely contains nested per-month zips and/or multi-part CSVs (e.g. 2023MM-citibike-tripdata_1.csv) - inspect the listing and extract recursively with Python zipfile into a fresh subdirectory; ignore __MACOSX and non-CSV entries. 2024 months are also likely split into several CSV parts - glob all parts. Open all archives with Python (never run interpreters from inside the download directories; run python with -I for scripts that read untrusted data, passing paths as arguments). (3) Inspect the schema of a sample from each year. Expected (post-2021 schema): ride_id, rideable_type, started_at, ended_at, start_station_name, start_station_id, end_station_name, end_station_id, start_lat, start_lng, end_lat, end_lng, member_casual. Check whether 2023 and 2024 columns/ timestamp formats match; read all columns as text first (station ids are mixed text/numeric) and parse timestamps explicitly. (4) Convert every CSV part to one parquet file per year (/app/parquet/trips_2023.parquet, trips_2024.parquet) with DuckDB read_csv (all_varchar then cast, union_by_name=true, store a source_file column). (5) Write /app/output/tables/data_manifest.json recording: URLs, file sizes, sha256 of each downloaded zip, list of CSV parts, schema, raw row count per source file and per year, min/max started_at. Check: every one of the 24 months (Jan-Dec 2023 and 2024) has a non-trivial row count (expect roughly 2-5 M rows in summer months and >=1M in winter months; flag any month far outside this); total row counts are consistent between CSV parts and parquet. STOP RULE: if a file cannot be downloaded or a month is missing after retries, do not fabricate or substitute data - write the shortfall to the manifest and a file /app/output/DATA_UNAVAILABLE.md explaining exactly what is missing, then continue only with the months/years actually obtained (a single complete year is acceptable per the brief). Delete the raw zips/CSVs after successful parquet conversion only if disk gets tight (112 GB free is plenty).
parameters.resources: CPU only; ~15 GB download, ~40 GB peak disk; 30-50 min mostly network-bound

experiments.skill_used: Clean trip records and build aggregate tables with DuckDB

parameters.description: Write /app/code/02_clean_aggregate.py (DuckDB over the parquet files from acquire-data). Parse started_at/ended_at as timestamps (they are NYC local wall-clock time; do not tz-shift, but note DST: the 1-hour 'spring forward' and duplicated 'fall back' hour can distort individual hours slightly - mention in limitations). Apply a documented, ordered set of cleaning rules and record how many rows each rule removes (a row is attributed to the FIRST rule it fails, but also report each rule's independent count): R1 missing or unparseable started_at or ended_at; R2 duplicate ride_id (keep one); R3 duration <= 0 s (negative or zero); R4 duration < 60 s (very short trips, commonly false starts/re-docks - report this as a separate, clearly labelled rule so the effect can be judged; the primary analysis excludes them, and a sensitivity check keeps them); R5 duration > 24 h (extreme/stuck/lost bikes); R6 started_at outside the calendar year of its file (e.g. a few trips that spill into the next/previous month or year - keep trips whose start is within Jan 1 2023-Dec 31 2024 and drop the rest); R7 missing/invalid member_casual (anything other than 'member' or 'casual'). Do NOT drop rows for missing station ids/coordinates (many dockless e-bike trips lack stations; report the share of missing station ids as a descriptive stat only). Write /app/output/tables/cleaning_summary.csv (rule, rows removed independent, rows removed sequential, % of raw, per year) and a per-month table of raw vs clean counts. Then produce aggregate tables from the clean data and save them as CSV in /app/output/tables/: (a) monthly_counts.csv (year, month, member_casual, trips, mean/median duration); (b) daily_counts.csv (date, year, month, dow, is_weekend, member_casual, trips) - this feeds the weather job; (c) hourly_dow.csv (year, month, date, dow, hour, member_casual, trips) at date x hour x user-type granularity so that day-level bootstrap CIs can be computed downstream; (d) duration summary by user type and rideable_type (classic_bike/electric_bike/docked_bike if present). Also record the rideable_type mix by year/month and member_casual share by year, to support the limitations section (the rider-type definition and bike-type mix change over time). Checks: sequential removals + clean rows = raw rows; sum of daily_counts per month equals monthly_counts; no date outside range; 365 + 366 = 731 distinct dates (2024 is a leap year); report any date with an implausibly low count (e.g. <10% of the median, Hurricane/snow days are real, outages are suspicious) in a short anomalies note.
parameters.resources: CPU only; DuckDB with threads=32; <20 min

experiments.skill_used: Analyse seasonal, weekday/hour and member-vs-casual patterns with figures and uncertainty

parameters.description: Write /app/code/03_temporal_analysis.py using pandas/matplotlib/scipy on the aggregate tables from clean-and-aggregate (invoke the dataviz skill guidance if available: clear labels, colorblind-safe palette, consistent colours for member/casual, 2023 vs 2024 shown as separate lines/panels). Produce, as PNG (dpi>=150) plus the underlying CSV for each: Q1 SEASONALITY - fig_monthly_volume.png: monthly trips for each year (and member/casual stacked or as two lines); table of peak month, trough month, peak/trough ratio per year, and each month's share of annual trips; check whether peak/trough months agree across 2023 and 2024; because months differ in length, also show trips per day (monthly trips / days in month). Uncertainty: monthly totals are census counts, so there is no sampling error - instead quantify between-day variability (mean daily trips +/- 95% bootstrap CI across days in each month) and year-to-year consistency (2023 vs 2024 monthly ratio). Q2 DAY-OF-WEEK x HOUR - fig_hourly_weekday_vs_weekend.png: mean trips per hour of day, weekday (Mon-Fri) vs weekend (Sat-Sun), one panel per year, with 95% bootstrap CI bands (resample dates, 2000 resamples) computed from per-date hourly counts; fig_heatmap_dow_hour.png: heatmap of mean trips by day-of-week x hour; table of the AM and PM peak hours (argmax within 6-10 and 15-20 on weekdays), their peak/midday ratio, and the weekend single midday/afternoon peak hour. Exclude/flag US federal holidays (use a hard-coded list or pandas USFederalHolidayCalendar) from the 'weekday' group in a sensitivity version and report if conclusions change. Check seasonal robustness by repeating the hourly profile for a summer month (e.g. Jul-Aug) and a winter month (Jan-Feb) - small table or panel. Q3 MEMBER vs CASUAL - fig_member_vs_casual_hourly.png (weekday and weekend panels, each user type normalised to its own share of daily trips so shapes are comparable, plus a raw-count version), fig_member_vs_casual_seasonal.png (casual share of trips by month, with the monthly casual share table), and a table of: share of trips on weekends by type, ratio of weekday AM+PM-peak trips to total, median trip duration by type (with bootstrap CI of the median from a duration sample read via DuckDB, e.g. 1M random trips per type per year, fixed seed), and a simple quantitative contrast of profile shape (e.g. the Jensen-Shannon distance or correlation between the two normalised hourly profiles, weekday vs weekend). Write /app/output/tables/findings_numbers.json containing every key number to be quoted in the report (peak/trough months and values, ratios, peak hours, shares, CIs). Describe, don't explain causally. Checks: figures open without error and look sensible (view them with the Read tool as images); totals in the figures match monthly_counts.csv; results are reported for both years and the same-direction replication is stated explicitly (or the difference noted).

Analysis: (1) scatter of daily trips vs mean temperature (colour by weekday/weekend, one panel per year or coloured by year), with a LOWESS curve; (2) boxplot / bar of daily trips by precipitation bin (0, 0-2.5, 2.5-10, >10 mm); (3) Spearman correlations (with bootstrap CI) of daily trips vs temperature and vs precipitation, overall and separately for member and casual, weekday and weekend; (4) an OLS (or log-linear) regression of log daily trips on temperature (and a quadratic temperature term or spline), a wet-day indicator/precipitation, day-of-week and holiday indicators, with HAC (Newey-West, ~7 lags) standard errors because daily series are autocorrelated, reporting the adjusted-temperature and rain coefficients as percent differences with 95% CI; compare with the unadjusted correlation to show how much of the temperature association is shared with the seasonal/ calendar structure. parameters.description: Read all outputs from earlier jobs (findings_numbers.json, weather_numbers.json if present, cleaning_summary.csv, data_manifest.json, figures) and write /app/output/report.md (short: roughly 2-4 pages, plus figures referenced by relative path figures/xxx.png; also render /app/output/report.html with embedded images or relative links if easy). Structure: (1) Summary - 3 to 5 findings in one sentence each; (2) Data and methods - source (Citi Bike system data, s3.amazonaws.com/tripdata, files used, retrieval date), years used, cleaning rules with the exact number and percentage of records removed per rule (from cleaning_summary.csv), and how uncertainty was computed (day-level bootstrap CIs, HAC errors); (3) Findings - each with one figure or table and the key numbers with uncertainty, e.g. F1 seasonal peak/trough month and ratio (replicated across 2023 and 2024); F2 weekday bimodal commute peaks (AM/PM hours) vs weekend single midday/afternoon hump; F3 member vs casual differences (commute-shaped and more weekday-weighted vs leisure-shaped, weekend- and summer-weighted, shorter vs longer trips); F4 (only if the weather job produced results and the association is clear) daily trips vs temperature/precipitation described as an association, not causation; a fifth finding only if well supported (e.g. year-over-year change, or e-bike share). The cleaning script ran to completion and all the expected output files exist and are non-empty. Every internal check passed.

Of the 79,410,195 raw trips (35.1M in 2023, 44.3M in 2024), 79,371,599 are kept. That is 99.95%, with 38,596 removed, counting each row against the first rule it fails.

| Rule | Removed (first rule failed) | Removed (rule alone) |
|---|---|---|
| R1 missing timestamps | 0 | 0 |
| R2 duplicate ride_id | 0 | 0 |
| R3 duration ≤ 0 s | 643 | 643 |
| R4 duration < 60 s | 182 | 825 |
| R5 duration > 24 h | 37,576 | 37,576 |
| R6 start outside 2023–2024 | 195 | 276 |
| R7 invalid member_casual | 0 | 0 |

- **R3 is a DST artifact, not bad data.** All 643 negative durations fall on the two fall-back dates, 2023-11-05 and 2024-11-03, where the repeated 01:00 hour makes some trips look negative.
- **Other DST effects.** The hour 02 bin is empty on the two spring-forward dates. The hour 01 bin is roughly doubled on the fall-back dates. Both are in the anomalies note.
- **R4 is small.** It removes 182 rows, so dropping versus keeping short trips changes almost nothing. The sensitivity columns (`trips_incl_short`) are in the aggregate tables.
- **R6 rows** are all December 2022 starts in the 2023 January file. Trips that start on 2023-12-31 sit in the 2024 January file and are kept, counted by their actual start time.

**Checks:**
- Sequential removals plus clean rows equal raw rows, overall and by year.
- Daily counts sum to the monthly counts, and hourly counts sum to the daily counts.
- There are 731 distinct dates (365 + 366), and the clean start times run from 2023-01-01 to 2024-12-31.
- No day falls below 10% of the median, so none is flagged as a suspected outage. The lowest day is 2023-04-29, a Saturday, at 16% of the median.

**Data notes for the report:**
- There are no `docked_bike` trips in this data, only classic and electric bikes.
- The electric share rose from 50.2% in 2023 to 66.1% in 2024.
- The casual share rose slightly, from 18.8% to 19.3%.
- Missing station ids are about 0.1%, all on electric bikes.
- Each trip is counted by its start time, not by the month of its source file. About 1,000 trips in some months differ between the two views.

**Uncertain:**
- I did not check the low-volume days against weather, holidays or outage records. That is left to the weather job.
- R5 removed more trips in 2023 (26,640) than in 2024 (10,936). I haven't investigated why.
- The first run was OOM-killed in the container, which has an 8 GB limit. I rebuilt the duration step to run one grouping at a time, and the final run ran clean.

ked. A command to copy the PNGs to the host for the Read tool was denied, and I did not try another route. I confirmed only that each file exists at 170 dpi and was drawn directly from `monthly_counts.csv`. The palette validator was also blocked, so I used the skill's published blue/orange for member/casual and its other documented palette colours elsewhere, unvalidated. Please open the figures once.

- **Script:** `/app/code/03_temporal_analysis.py`, log in `/app/output/03_temporal_analysis.log`. It reads the existing aggregate tables and takes about 40 seconds. A copy is in the host `workspace/`.
- **Figures:** the five requested PNGs plus `fig_hourly_seasonal_robustness.png`, which shows winter vs summer hourly profiles.
- **Tables:** `seasonality_summary.csv`, `peak_hours.csv`, `member_casual_summary.csv`, `findings_numbers.json`, and about ten supporting CSVs, one behind each figure.
- **Checks:** monthly totals match `monthly_counts.csv` for both years. The hourly, daily and monthly tables each sum to 79,371,599 clean trips.

**Findings** (all numbers are in `findings_numbers.json`):
- **Seasonality:** Volume peaks in a broad summer–autumn plateau and is lowest in winter.
  - The peak/trough ratio is about 2.3 to 2.7 for trips per month, or 2.2 to 2.7 for trips per day.
  - The trough is January in 2024 and February in 2023 (January on a per-day basis).
  - The exact peak month differs between years (August 2023, October 2024 on monthly totals; August vs September on trips per day). Bootstrap agreement on the peak month is only 55% to 88%, so the peak month is not well pinned down.
  - 2024 volume is 1.26 times 2023, and the 2024/2023 ratio is above 1 in every month, so the winter-low/summer-high shape is the same in both years.
- **Commute peaks:** On weekdays there is an 08:00 and a 17:00 peak in both years, and 100% of resamples agree on both hours. The 08:00 peak is about 1.5 times the midday level and the 17:00 peak about 2.0 times. Excluding federal holidays shifts those ratios by 0.03 to 0.04 and leaves the peak hours unchanged. All four daylight-saving dates fall on Sundays, so that sensitivity affects only the weekend profile.
- **Weekends:** Weekends have a single midday/afternoon peak, at 15:00 in both years. It is a broad plateau: in 2024, 54% to 73% of resamples agree on 15:00 (the 2024 Jan–Feb peak falls at 14:00).
- **Day of week:** Within-week, Sunday is the lowest day at about 0.85 to 0.88 of the weekly mean. The weekday ordering is not consistent between years.
- **Member vs casual:**
  - **Weekend share:** Casual riders have a larger share of trips on weekends (35.4% vs 23.3% for members in 2023; the same pattern holds in 2024).
  - **Weekday profile:** Casual riders show no distinct morning peak and a smaller evening peak. The weekday hourly profiles differ moderately (Jensen-Shannon distance about 0.12) and the weekend profiles are nearly identical (about 0.06).
  - **Seasonality:** Casual trips are far more seasonal, with a peak/trough ratio of 3.9 to 5.5 versus about 2.0 to 2.5 for members. Casual share of trips runs from about 11% in winter to 23% in summer.
  - **Duration:** The median casual trip is about 1.6 times as long as the median member trip (13.1 to 13.8 vs 8.3 to 8.6 minutes). The 1M-trip samples reproduce the full-population medians to within 0.02 minutes.

**Uncertainty and limitations:**
- **What the intervals measure:** The confidence intervals capture between-day variability only. Monthly totals are census counts, and there is no weather adjustment.
- **Calendar effects:** Months differ in the number of weekends, which I did not adjust for.

I fetched daily Central Park weather for 2023-01-01 to 2024-12-31 from Open-Meteo (HTTP 200, 731 days, no missing values). I joined it to the cleaned daily trip counts and ran the analysis in `/app/code/04_weather.py`. The log is `/app/output/04_weather.log`. Temperature is in °C and precipitation in mm. All numbers below are associations, not causal effects.

**Findings**
- **Temperature:** daily trips rise with warmth (Spearman ρ = 0.73, 95% block-bootstrap CI 0.62–0.78). The link is stronger for casual riders (0.81) than for members (0.66). Weekdays and weekends look alike (0.74 and 0.73).
- **Precipitation:** trips fall on wetter days (ρ = −0.29, CI −0.38 to −0.19).
- **Temperature, adjusted:** in the model with day-of-week, holiday, year and rain (HAC standard errors, 7 lags), trips rise about 38% per +10 °C from 10 to 20 °C. They rise about 11% per +10 °C from 20 to 30 °C (95% CI 3–19%). The fitted curve flattens near 29 °C.
- **Rain, relative to a dry day:** trips are 9% lower on days with 0–2.5 mm (CI −11 to −6%). They are 23% lower on days with 2.5–10 mm (CI −27 to −19%) and 42% lower on days over 10 mm (CI −48 to −36%).
- **Season:** the temperature association is mostly shared with seasonal and calendar structure. Temperature alone gives R² 0.50 on log trips. Calendar terms alone give 0.11, month fixed effects plus calendar 0.62, and the full model 0.80.
- **Within-month check:** with month fixed effects, temperature is identified only from day-to-day variation inside a month. The effect is still about +3.7% per °C (CI 3.0–4.4%), close to the unadjusted 3.7% per °C. Without the rain terms it is smaller, about 3.1% per °C. Rain is cooler on average, so leaving it out understates the temperature effect.

**Uncertainty**
- **Autocorrelation:** residuals are still autocorrelated (Durbin-Watson 1.15), so confidence intervals may be somewhat optimistic. Widening the HAC window to 14 lags raises the temperature standard error from 0.0036 to 0.0042.
- **Weather proxy:** Open-Meteo gives gridded reanalysis values for one point, used as a stand-in for city-wide weather. Daily totals also lose when in the day the rain fell.
- **Confounding:** other seasonal factors (daylight, school calendar, tourism) can't be separated from temperature, even with month fixed effects.
- **Year effect:** mean daily trips were about 96k in 2023 and 121k in 2024. The models include a year indicator, but the weather figures don't separate it out.

open_questions: The 2023 data came from the yearly zip, not the monthly files (monthly 2023 URLs return 404), so equivalence with the original monthly files is unverified. Row counts and date ranges look plausible.
R5 (duration > 24h) removed 26,640 trips in 2023 vs 10,936 in 2024 and this was not investigated. It is below 0.08% of trips, so it does not change any finding.

Casual vs member is the system's label, whose definition may have changed over time; it is not verified here and cannot be checked within these two years.

claims.statement: Monthly volume is strongly seasonal: lowest in winter (Jan/Feb), highest in a broad summer-autumn plateau. Peak/trough ratio is about 2.3 (2023) and 2.7 (2024) on monthly totals, and 2.2 (CI 2.07-2.42) and 2.7 (CI 2.49-3.14) per day. The exact peak month is not well pinned down (Aug 2023, Oct 2024 by totals; bootstrap agreement 55-88%). 2024 exceeds 2023 in every month (about 1.26x overall).

Weekdays show two commute peaks, at 08:00 and 17:00, in both years (100% of bootstrap resamples agree). The 08:00 peak is about 1.5x the 11-14h midday mean and the 17:00 peak about 2.0x (2023: 1.46 and 1.97; 2024: 1.54 and 2.04). Excluding federal holidays shifts ratios by only 0.03-0.04. Weekends have a single broad midday/afternoon peak, centred at 15:00 (a plateau, 54-98% bootstrap agreement depending on year/season). Weekend days are less busy than weekdays on average, and Sunday is the lowest day of the week (about 0.85-0.88 of the weekly mean).
supporting_evidence: my re-query of 2024 clean trips: member weekday top hours 17,18,8; weekend 15,14,13

claims.statement: Members and casual riders differ. Casual riders take a larger share of trips on weekends (35.4% vs 23.3% for members in 2023, similar in 2024; CIs do not overlap). On weekdays members have both an 08:00 and a 17:00 peak, while casual riders have a weak or absent morning peak and a smaller evening peak. Weekday profile distance is moderate (Jensen-Shannon about 0.12), weekend profiles are nearly identical (about 0.06). Casual riding is much more seasonal (casual peak/trough about 4.4 in 2023 and 5.4 in 2024, vs about 2.1 and 2.5 for members). Casual trips are also longer (median about 13-14 min vs about 8.4-8.6 for members).
supporting_evidence: my re-query: casual weekday 2024 top hours 17,18,16 (08:00 not in top 3)

claims.statement: Daily trip counts are positively associated with temperature (Spearman rho 0.73, block-bootstrap CI 0.62-0.78; casual 0.81, member 0.66) and negatively with precipitation (rho -0.29, CI -0.38 to -0.19). In an adjusted log model, relative to dry days trips are about 9% lower on 0-2.5 mm days, 23% lower on 2.5-10 mm, and 42% lower above 10 mm. The temperature effect is nonlinear (about +38% per +10C from 10 to 20C, about +11% from 20 to 30C). Within-month the temperature coefficient stays about +3.7%/C, so the association is not only shared seasonality, but season (daylight, school, tourism) cannot be fully separated. Association only, not causal.

Data cleaning removed only 38,596 of 79,410,195 raw trips (0.049%; 27,230 in 2023, 11,366 in 2024). Dominant rule is duration > 24h (37,576). The 643 negative-duration rows are all on the two fall-back DST dates (artifact of repeated 01:00 hour), not bad data. Findings are insensitive to cleaning: dropping or keeping the sub-60s trips changes 182 rows.

Which month is the single peak, and which weekday is busiest, are not robust: the peak month changes between years and between total vs per-day measures, and the weekday ordering is not consistent between years. Reports should describe a summer-autumn plateau rather than name one peak month.
